articles.content_orig:
Get Mike Santoli's Market Memo in your inbox first. SUBSCRIBE HERE
In a previous life, when I routinely shut down New York City bars, the end of Daylight Saving Time was an annual bonus, as 2am on a Saturday night instantly became 1am, leaving three more hours until closing time.
The financial markets now are undergoing several forms of late-cycle unease, and Wall Street is now looking for earnings season and the passage of the midterm elections to turn back the clock before last call.
To be clear, this remains a bull market, the S&P 500 's uptrend unbroken, with constant rotations between AI tech and remainder of the market fitfully supporting the tape, with pullbacks limited to 3% for half a year.
Still, the index is now chopping around a flattish 50-day moving average at levels first reached 11 weeks ago, the AI-hardware cohort has badly broken stride, bank stocks are trading poorly off their results, and credit markets are getting colicky.
Late last week, the urgent selling in semiconductors and data-center equities and debt resembled the sort of forced-unwind rhythms from July, when a big upstart tech hedge fund was in the process of being all but liquidated.
A tentative bounce in semiconductor stocks Monday was minimally reassuring, in that it meant we didn't get the further disorderly purge many had braced for over the weekend (when S&P 500 "perpetual" futures on Hyperliquid had a sudden head-fake drop late Saturday).
Jason Hunter, technical strategist at JP Morgan, sets out the crucial question for a market sending mixed signals:
"With the bearish seasonal window now closing, we are left wondering if the market is in the terminal phase of a sequence of rolling corrections ahead of a typical late-year rally. Or are the plentiful amounts of bearish internal, momentum, and intra-market divergences that have formed as the S&P 500 index has decelerated below longer-term channel resistance setting the market up for a larger and more correlated setback?"
He leans toward a more cautious interpretation, keeping the S&P 500 on a short leash that extends about 2.5% lower to 7500, a break of which would lose the tape the benefit of the doubt.
Based on precedent and circumstance, the market "should" be setting up for a comeback that could reset the clock in bulls' favor. The fourth quarter after a midterm election year, historically, is overwhelmingly positive. Earnings growth projected to exceed a 20% year-over-year growth rate again this quarter can hardly be viewed as anything but a positive at least to bolster the fundamental case.
Still, against most probabilities, 2018 happened. By which I mean a 19% S&P 500 peak-to-trough decline in the fourth quarter of a midterm-election year, one that saw total S&P 500 earnings grow by more than 20%.
The 2018 tailspin had followed a massive momentum crescendo and reversal several months earlier, which gave way to an erratic tape that couldn't absorb what seemed at the time relatively unthreatening Federal Reserve tightening actions.
Financial conditions have now been tightening by means of higher Treasury yields, somewhat wider corporate-credit spreads, an uptick in volatility and a stronger U.S. dollar.
It's become common to hear investors insist that "the market is doing the Fed's tightening for it," suggesting Chairman Kevin Warsh himself should show restraint in further hiking rates despite the recent upturn in inflation. Sure, but the reason the markets are tightening is, in part, because Warsh himself expressed resolve in fighting inflation and investors therefore believe he'll take short-term rates up a bit more.
How Warsh treats these market shifts after next week's Fed meeting is another node of disagreement on the Street.
Bank of America economist Aditya Bhave says the markets are testing the Fed's pain threshold with the Nasdaq retreating 5% and credit spreads flaring a bit. The market has taken recent Fedspeak to suggest very low chances of an October rate hike, even though Warsh himself has decried forward guidance and said the Fed shouldn't suppress normal market volatility. Bhave is maintaining his non-consensus prediction for an October hike, conceding it's a close call.
Morgan Stanley equity strategist Mike Wilson takes the other side on the Fed's response to the recent tensing up of markets: "We think some acknowledgement of this tightening by Warsh would be well received by rate-sensitive areas that have already derated notably. Conversely, an indifference to this tightening may invoke memories of Powell's 2018 'auto-pilot' remarks in reference to that tightening episode."
The "de-rating" and "de-risking" process has surely been notable in recent weeks, with small and cyclical stocks under significant valuation pressure and hedge funds aggressively repositioning out of tech.
Is it enough to enliven buyers into or after the election?
Ned Davis Research thematic strategist Pat Tschosik notes his firm's proprietary market-breadth reading Big Mo Tape tentatively turning higher from oversold readings. "If Big Tech disappoints on Q3 earnings, we may get a full market washout and Big Mo could head even lower like it did in October 2023. Perhaps this is what is needed to set up for a post-midterm-election rally into yearend."
John Kolovos of Macro Risk Advisors sees a similar level to JPMorgan's as the market's breaking point, while evaluating his sentiment indicator.
Kolovos on the latest reading: "A noticeable sentiment reset is underway on the heels of the AI trade unwind and tightening financial conditions.  The good news is that bullish sentiment is finally starting to wash out, which should set the stage for a year-end rally. However, a break below the mid-September lows on the S&P 500 near 7,500 would warn that something more than a routine pullback is unfolding."
-There's something of a paradox at work – or a collective investor blind spot - when the bond market is finally offering relatively safe income after many years of meager yields and yet people continue to rush for the engineered income delivered by options-selling ETFs. This CNBC.com piece offers a thorough, smart rundown of these strategies, complete with warnings of tax pitfalls. This Bloomberg report details a more aggressive approach through funds many investors don't quite understand, while introducing me to the community of self-styled "dividend nomads."
-Anthropic's proposal to place 5% of its equity into a "public benefit fund" to help groups potentially disadvantaged by AI's propagation and Elon Musk's stated offer to give one of his SpaceX shares to every American child via Trump Accounts suggest that anxiety over AI economic disruption is going from simmer to boil.
We can cynically observe that such efforts also hype these companies' world-changing potency, a form of marketing through scare-mongering sheathed in generosity.  But the concern over AI's impact on current worker groups is well-placed, even if ultimately society adapts around step-function technological change. The best hedge against AI-powered capital overtaking labor is arguably to own more capital, whether through the S&P 500 or other vehicles.
Or one could raise the value of one's human capital, through training or becoming excellent at something. This has always been Warren Buffett's answer for how one should become inflation-resistant, as he detailed at Berkshire Hathaway's annual meeting a few years ago , at the height of the pandemic inflation surge.
Bull markets can keep rolling for a long while after they've become fully embraced and stocks are no longer cheap. But I find myself cataloguing various ways that the cushions against adverse surprises are getting worn pretty flat.
Here's the running tally of investors' collective cash holdings as a percentage of total margin debt. It's running well below the levels of the year 2000 at this point.

Qatar and Pakistan have presented Washington and Tehran with a compromise proposal aimed at preventing renewed escalation and bringing the two sides back to the negotiating table, Qatari outlet Al-Araby Al-Jadeed reported, citing informed sources.
The initiative was met with U.S. approval and a positive response from Iran, the outlet reported.
The proposal was conveyed to Iranian officials by Pakistan's army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, who arrived in Tehran on Tuesday at the head of a delegation of Pakistani officials, according to the report.
The suggested arrangement includes a partial response to Iran's demand for the release of frozen assets. Under the initiative, Iran would receive interest generated by $6 billion in Iranian funds frozen in Qatari banks, the sources said.
In return, Tehran has reportedly agreed to an undisclosed visit by the International Atomic Energy Agency to Iranian nuclear sites, addressing a key U.S. demand concerning Iran's nuclear program.
The sources said a potential breakthrough could be announced this week.
An Iranian military official said Tuesday that Tehran is pursuing legal action over the U.S. torpedo attack on the IRIS Dena warship, arguing the vessel was not a legitimate military target.
In early March, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said a torpedo launched from a U.S. Navy submarine had sunk an Iranian warship in the Indian Ocean "that thought it was safe in international waters."
"Instead it was sunk by a torpedo — quiet death," Hegseth said. It was the first time a U.S. Navy submarine had used a torpedo to sink a warship since 1945.
The strike killed more than 80 Iranian service members.
In an interview with Iranian state TV on Tuesday, Brig. Gen. Moslem Yaghoubi, the Iranian army deputy for legal affairs, said the vessel was an unarmed training ship carrying trainees and that it was hit about 1,200 miles from the battlefield.
"Just this one point is enough to establish that striking it was militarily unnecessary," he said.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in June that Iran was collating documents related to the incident for what state media described as "legal follow-up," but Tehran has not specified a court in which it intends to file its legal action.
Saudi Arabia said Tuesday it had intercepted a drone targeting Riyadh, as well as a missile it previously said was taken down.
Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen, said on X that a drone had also been intercepted and destroyed, without specifying who was believed to have launched it.
The bulletin came after the country's Civil Defense said earlier that people in the Riyadh area should "avoid crowds or going to dangerous areas, and refrain from taking photos" in a post on X , before saying the danger had passed .
Shortly after, Al-Maliki said a ballistic missile launched by the Iran-backed Houthis at Riyadh had been " intercepted and destroyed ."
French President Emmanuel Macron has secured the delivery of an additional 200,000 tons of diesel per month from the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain during a tour of the Persian Gulf, the French presidency said Tuesday.
He obtained commitments for around 100,000 tons per month from the UAE, and an additional 100,000 tons from Bahrain, the French Elysee presidential palace said, according to the AFP news agency.
With the addition of deliveries from Saudi Arabia, France has commitments for 295,000 tons per month, representing just over 10% of its consumption, the statement added.
Macron is undertaking a tour of key energy suppliers in the Gulf in an effort to secure oil and diesel and bring down prices in France after a weekend of violent protests over soaring living costs and other social issues.
The G7 countries, chaired this year by France, agreed in early October to release up to 100 million barrels of oil from their strategic reserves to ease pressure on global fuel supplies amid the U.S.-Iran war.
The shipments for France will be sent overland via Oman, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, the French presidency said. Experts have questioned whether the deliveries will have an impact on prices in France, however, given the risk of renewed fighting in the region.
Iran's Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces warned Tuesday that Tehran would not wait for the U.S. midterm elections before retaliating to any new U.S. attack.
Maj. Gen. Abdollahi said Iran "has not waited, nor will it wait, for the results of the U.S. congressional elections" to respond to any new attack.
He blamed regional insecurity on the presence of U.S. forces and warned countries hosting American troops to remain vigilant.
"Countries hosting the United States in the region should also know that the main cause of insecurity in the region is the presence of the terrorist U.S. military," he said.
The U.K. government announced Tuesday that it is expanding military support for Saudi Arabia as it faces ongoing attacks by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, including "defensive" air patrols by British Royal Air Force jets over the kingdom.
Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said Royal Air Force Typhoon jets would "conduct defensive counter-air operations over Saudi Arabia, helping to protect Saudi cities, civilian populations and critical national infrastructure from Houthi attack."
He said British planes would not strike Houthi targets in Yemen.
The U.K. will also send a military transport plane and an unspecified number of military advisers to Saudi Arabia, Streeting said.
The announcement follows Britain's decision last month to offer in-air refueling of Saudi planes operating against the Iran-backed rebels. That mission is being extended by another 90 days, Streeting said.
The death toll from a Houthi missile strike on a government military camp in southern Yemen rose to 73 people Tuesday, making it the deadliest strike since fighting in the country began escalating three months ago, a senior Yemeni government official said Tuesday.
The recruits were all aged between 18 and 20, and some were still missing a day after the Iran-backed Houthis hit the al-Alam camp in the southern province of Shabwa with ballistic missiles, according to provincial governor Awad Ibn al-Wazir.
Negotiations between Iran and the United States are ongoing despite rising tension and repeated statements from President Trump that the U.S. could resume major strikes on Iran next month, Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari said Tuesday.
"The negotiation is ongoing. We are seeing engagement from the parties," al-Ansari, who also serves as an adviser to Qatar's prime minister, said at the Global Security Forum in Doha on Tuesday.
Al-Ansari did not offer any further information on the negotiations, including whether there have been any recent direct contacts between Iranian and U.S. officials or if the talks are being conducted entirely via mediators.
He said discussions were continuing with regional partners and expressed hope that diplomatic efforts would eventually lead to an agreement, while cautioning that conditions on the ground were becoming increasingly difficult.
"Escalation left unchecked will mean that we are spiraling towards a regional war that will expand beyond the borders of our region," he warned.

articles.title_orig: China ramps up cyberattacks for potential election meddling: officials
articles.title_zh: China ramps up cyberattacks for potential election meddling: officials
articles.content_orig:
The Government Service Network (GSN) reported a surge of 185.6 million cyberattacks in July, suggesting that Beijing could be preparing large-scale interference operations ahead of the Nov. 28 elections, government officials said.
Cyberattacks on the network, likely originating in China, spiked between June and last month, the National Security Bureau (NSB) said in a report submitted to the Legislative Yuan for a meeting scheduled for tomorrow.
As of last month, the GSN was attacked 2.58 million times a day on average, and the attacks reported in July exceeded the sum of total cyberattacks in the first quarter this year, the document said.
Cyberattacks exceeded 100 million in three months last year: during the anniversary of President William Lai’s (賴清德) inauguration in April (100 million), in May (about 300 million) and during Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim’s (蕭美琴) visit to Europe in November (about 200 million), it said.
The NSB cannot rule out the possibility that the July attacks are part of Beijing’s plan to meddle in next month’s nine-in-one elections, the report said, adding that the agency had warned of the same in April.
Chinese hackers in the first half of the year targeted academic institutions, telecommunications and defense industry supply chains as part of a long war against Taiwan’s critical infrastructure, it said.
The attacks were aimed at disrupting Taiwan’s ability to govern and direct national defense policy, its collaboration with other governments and the theft of sensitive technology, it said.
Beijing-directed cyberwarfare continues to improve in sophistication and artificial intelligence (AI) technology has been deployed in hacks, it said.
AI is utilized across various stages of a cyberattack, including probing for weaknesses, target seeking, searching for zero-day exploits and malware attacks via e-mail, the report said.
Automation has increased Chinese hackers’ operational tempo and their efficiency in finding gaps in Taiwan’s defenses and identifying targets for infiltration, it said.
Meanwhile, the NSB said it believes that Beijing would leverage technology and human intelligence to craft a strategy to influence next month’s elections, targeting Taiwan’s domestic wedge issues such as energy, food safety and national defense, and using fake polls and reports about the races, and AI-generated content, it said.
Suspicious social media accounts made 2.5 million posts containing controversial or disputed information from January to last month, up 48 percent compared with 1.69 million in the same period last year, the report said.
The method and platform for spreading cognitive warfare posts included content farms, AI-generated video or audio content, and brigading the comment section on platforms, forums and other Web sites, it said.
Facebook and Threads accounted for 68.9 percent and 9 percent respectively of all controversial content from suspicious accounts, it said.
Suspicious posts on Facebook and Threads were up by 25.3 and 4.5 percentage points from last year respectively, indicating China’s increasing preference for using these platforms, the report said.
AI is playing an increasingly prominent role in Beijing’s informational operations, it said.
China’s strategy for manipulating Taiwanese public opinion follows the model of using official outlets to craft narratives, which are then amplified by troll, bot and public relations company-owned accounts, the report said.

articles.title_orig: GM Plans $20 Billion in Buybacks, but Warns of Bumpy 2027
articles.title_zh: GM Plans $20 Billion in Buybacks, but Warns of Bumpy 2027
articles.content_orig:
DETROIT — General Motors narrowed its 2026 earnings guidance and raised its free cash flow expectations after beating Wall Street's third-quarter expectations.
The Detroit automaker also announced a new multiyear stock buyback of $20 billion after GM completed a $6 billion share repurchase program that was announced in January. GM did not disclose a specific time to complete the program.
Despite the positive news, GM stock was off roughly 5% during trading Tuesday as the company's outlook missed Wall Street's expectations.
Wall Street analysts were mixed before the report on whether GM would raise its guidance Tuesday amid concerns of slowing sales and rising commodity costs. Analysts' expectations included a midpoint of $13.41 per share for the year compared with GM's new $13.25 per share midpoint, according to LSEG.
Several analysts in investor notes Tuesday said GM's third-quarter results were solid, but raised concerns about whether higher costs and pressures on vehicle pricing would limit earnings growth next year.
Here's how GM performed in the third quarter, compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG:
GM's new guidance includes adjusted earnings before interest and taxes of between $14.5 billion and $15.5 billion, or $12.75 to $13.75 adjusted earnings per share, and adjusted automotive free cash flow of between $11.5 billion and $12.5 billion.
That compares with its raised guidance from July that included adjusted EBIT of between $14 billion and $16 billion, or $12 to $14 adjusted EPS, and adjusted automotive free cash flow of $9.5 billion to $11.5 billion.
"I think the market's been pretty consistent from what we've said all year," GM CFO Paul Jacobson told CNBC's Phil LeBeau . "Our fourth quarter's going to be down sequentially. ... I think the fact that we're able to hold our guidance in the face of that late inflationary pressure in the year is another sign of the GM team executing really well."
GM on Tuesday said it expects commodity inflation costs to be around $2 billion, which was the high end of its previous guidance. That includes higher costs for logistics and dynamic random-access memory, or DRAM, chips that are impacting multiple industries .
While the inflationary costs were at the automaker's high end of guidance, GM said its gross tariff costs are expected to be at the low end of its expected $2.5 billion to $3.5 billion range. Warranty costs are expected to be at high end between $1 billion and $1.5 billion, GM said.
Jacobson said vehicle pricing is relatively flat as inflationary costs continue to increase. He said the company would assess where consumers are in the coming year when deciding if it should pass costs along by raising prices more than normal.
"GM is performing well, and we are working hard to continue our momentum despite growing inflationary pressures through strategic investments in new products and services, and through improved quality and operating efficiency," GM CEO Mary Barra said Tuesday in a letter to shareholders.
The automaker also said the costs of its pullback in all-electric vehicles announced last year were "substantially completed," saying it has recorded $11.2 billion in such charges since the second half of last year, including paying $4.6 billion of $7.4 billion in cash through the third quarter.
The company's net income attributed to stockholders was $3.3 billion during the third quarter, up roughly $2 billion from a year earlier.
GM's North American operations continued to lead the automaker's results, accounting for $3.6 billion of its $4.1 billion in adjusted EBIT results during the third quarter.
GM's 2025 third-quarter results included $48.59 billion in revenue, net income attributable to stockholders of $1.3 billion and earnings per share of $2.80 adjusted.

And back to the debate in the French parliament, the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, confirmed that military forces will be deployed to reinforce police during the upcoming protests on Saturday.
“We will ⁠deploy the Sentinelle force, ​obviously ‌as a substitute ‌to interior security ‌forces... mostly to free police and gendarmes in their mission to maintain order,” Nuñez ‌told the National Assembly.
He added that the response to any unrest will be “firm.”
As reported earlier, PM Lecornu said the police presence on the weekend would be “massive,” as the government wants to see an immediate return to order after last weekend’s riots ( 15:29 ).
Asked about his confidence in doing deal with Trump, Zelenskyy is very diplomatic.
He goes back to his conversation with Rubio earlier today, and says it was the right channel to discuss “sensitive issues” such as Stalink, interceptors, and intelligence sharing.
He says he hopes to talk with Rubio again in the next 48 hours.
By the way, you can watch the Oslo briefing here:
In the Q&A, Ukraine’s Zelenskyy gets asked about his concessions and whether he is losing the war now.
He says the discussions revolved around “sensitive” issues, but he wants to “push as quick as possible to end this war” and focus next discussions on reconstruction.
He insists “we are not losing the war,” but concedes that “we are losing people and time,” as “our children do not have real life, childhood.”
He says “that is why we need to end this war as quick as possible.”
Finland’s Stubb says he believes today’s talks achieved some “genuine” progress “on two levels: … the short term and the big picture.”
“We found some elements of peace which will be taken forward to Saint Petersburg tomorrow.”
He says the discussions focused on “key issues such as air defence, energy installations, and partial ceasefires, such as those on energy and food security,” building on discussions in Miami.
Stubb says he understand “there has been a lot of noise” but “on a technical level, I feel that we are on the same page, and the next steps are about how we get there.”
“In my experience, peace requires patience, but unfortunately war does not wait. People are dying every day and each day. Our job is to do what we can to end it. And I think today was a step in the right direction.”
Ukraine’s Zelenskyy is up next.
He thanks Norway for hosting the talks, and Finland’s Stubb for joining the process.
He says today’s talk with the US were “important” as he says all parties need to “keep talking at all levels and work together on the decisions needed to end this war.”
He thanks US secretary of state Marco Rubio for their earlier phone call conversation, too.
“ Ukraine wants peace more than anyone. It was Russia who started this war, and the decision to keep the killing going is Russia’s choice and Russia’s alone.”
“We are working to find a solution. I thought we have some clear ideas on how to get to peace, and we are united with our European partners in this effort, and we want the Americans to take these ideas to the Russians.”
He says he wants a trilateral meeting of the leaders – that’s Trump, Putin and himself – because there are issues that “only the leaders” can resolve.
Norway’s Støre is the first to speak.
He says Norway remains supportive of Ukraine, and “we have always made it clear there will be nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine.”
He thanks Trump’s envoys Witkoff and Kushner for joining the talks, and says:
“We believe that peace is possible and necessary for Ukraine and for Europe and for the entire world. We have hosted today, I would say, good and constructive talks, necessary after events of the last week. We have agreed that working together is crucial.”
He says US’s Witkoff will fly to St. Petersburg tomorrow to relay the result of today’s proposals to Russia, and “possibly pave the way for a meeting at the leaders’ level.”
“We have discussed today issues linked to security for Ukraine, prosperity plan after the war; issues related to territory and issues related to sanctions and questions related to European security order in the aftermath of this war.”
Zelenskyy, Støre and Stubb are here.
We are now pausing our coverage as we wait for the Ukraine-US talks in Oslo to wrap up.
I will be back when the leaders of Ukraine, Norway and Finland show up for their press conference, which is currently expected around 6pm UK (7pm Oslo). We will bring you the presser live here.
In the meantime, here’s the summary of the day so far:
Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy is in Oslo, holding talks with the US peace envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, with the Norwegian PM Støre and Finnish president Stubb also attending ( 12:23 , 13:22 , 16:06 ).
French authorities said that military forces will be deployed to reinforce “massive” police presence during the upcoming protests on Saturday ( 15:29 , 15:57 ), as they framed the worsening situation as a choice between “violence and the Republic.”
Italian defence minister Guido Crosetto warned that city riots, seen also in the Italian city of Milan, are part of a broader “hybrid war” against the west, with younger people radicalising through the use of social media platforms ( 15:21 ), with the Italian government planning to approve new security measures ( 14:27 ).
EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said the bloc’s relationship with the UK is of “vital importance in the current geopolitical, security and economic context,” as he set out the bloc’s expectations ahead of next month’s EU-UK summit on 20 November ( 11:44 ).
Meanwhile, UN Human Rights chief Volker Türk has condemned “all acts of violence” during the last week’s protests in Albania, Belgium, France , Italy and Portugal, and called on all parties to “reduce tensions and prevent further violence.”
In a statement he insisted that “the best and only way forward is inclusive and safe dialogue.”
“ People have the right to protest peacefully, and to have their voices heard. States must facilitate these rights.
I deplore the actions of those exploiting protests to commit acts of violence and vandalism against public and private property. They should be held individually accountable.
I am concerned by reports of unnecessary and excessive use of force against protesters, including children. States must ensure that any law enforcement response remains lawful, necessary and proportionate. Allegations of unlawful use of force must be investigated promptly, effectively and independently, with accountability and effective remedies for victims.
I note some steps already taken by authorities to investigate incidents and ease tensions. I further urge States to engage protesters, particularly young people, in meaningful, inclusive and constructive dialogue, and to take concrete steps to address legitimate and fundamental human rights concerns over education, public services, housing, the rising cost of living and inequality.”
Kyiv mayor Vitaly Klitschko said that an energy facility in Kyiv was hit this afternoon, as Russian attacks on Ukraine continue.
No details were immediately available, but the attack fits the pattern of Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure in recent weeks.
Earlier today, Klitschko reported a number of other drone attacks in and around the capital, with at least one dead and nine injured.
Meanwhile, two men are appearing in a Danish court this afternoon for suspected espionage for Russian intelligence, the country’s public broadcaster DR reported.
A short press release issued by the police quoted the head of investigation at the North Jutland force saying that “this is a case we are taking very seriously.”
The case focuses on suspected cooperation with foreign intelligence and has been brought forward in partnership with the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, the police said, without disclosing more d

Surprise! Hot on the heels of PlayStation's own upscaling tech announcements, Microsoft and AMD just revealed that the firm's flagship FSR 4.1 tech is coming to the Xbox platform.
FSR (FidelityFX Super Resolution) is a technology from AMD that renders games at a lower resolution, and then uses machine learning to generate a sharper image. Since the hardware isn't working as hard, that overhead can be used for performance.
FSR 4.1 is a big leap over previous versions, and Microsoft has partnered with AMD to bring it not only to Xbox Series X , but also Xbox Ally X , Xbox Ally S and Xbox Series S — the latter two of which should benefit from very, very big performance boosts as a result.
"At Xbox, we're building a gaming platform designed to meet players where they are, and make it easier for creators to reach them," Xbox CTO Scott Van Vilet explained. "AMD has been an important partner in that journey for more than two decades. Together our teams have been pushing gaming forward, across Xbox and Windows. From the silicon at the heart of our consoles and handhelds, to technologies like DirectX, Advanced Shader Delivery, and AutoSR that helps developers get more from the hardware and deliver better experiences for our players."
"Today, we're excited to take another step forward together. With FSR 4.1 coming to Xbox. Now, we've worked very closely with AMD to optimize this technology, giving developers another powerful tool for great performance and visual quality for players. Now, whether you're playing on an Xbox Ally handheld, as well as coming soon to Xbox Series X and Series S consoles. And this is just the beginning. Our teams are continuing to work together across hardware and software, and there's even more ahead with Project Helix, leveraging FSR Diamond to power what comes next."
It's unclear exactly when these technologies will roll out to Xbox devices. It sounds as though FSR 4.1 will hit Xbox Ally X before the year end, but Xbox Series X|S are listed as "coming soon," with no exact window offered.
Sadly, it seems the Xbox Ally base model is fully incompatible with FSR 4.1, which is a bit of a shame, but it should prove transformative for those with the Xbox Ally X and the just-released Xbox Ally X20 , as well as the Xbox Series S.
UPDATE: I stand corrected, I just confirmed that it is also coming to the Xbox Ally base model as well!
The Xbox Series S has historically been difficult for developers owing to its irregular RAM allocation, but if FSR 4.1 can do some of the heavy lifting, it should ease the pressure on developers to deliver a native 1080p image.
We're reaching out to Microsoft for some clarification on timelines and will get back to you if we hear from them.

articles.title_orig: UK to send jets to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks, and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: UK to send jets to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks, and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
The United Kingdom said Tuesday it will deploy fighter jets to defend Saudi Arabia against attacks by the Iran-allied Houthi rebels in Yemen.
The UK will fly “defensive counter-air missions” using Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets to protect Saudi cities and critical infrastructure, the Defense Ministry said in a statement.
Over the past month, the Houthis have intensified their attacks on Saudi Arabia, launching ballistic missiles and drones at key infrastructure, including oil facilities and airports.
The UK is already providing air-to-air refueling support to Saudi Arabia and has deployed air defense equipment and British personnel to help protect the kingdom, a spokesperson for the prime minister’s office told reporters.
The Typhoons will intercept missiles and drones launched against Saudi Arabia and will not conduct offensive strikes inside Yemen, the spokesperson said.
The conflict has been intensifying since the Houthis announced in July that they would target Saudi shipping in the Red Sea as well as infrastructure inside the kingdom, following a Saudi attack on the Houthi-controlled airport in the Yemeni capital, Sanaa.
They have stepped up their attacks in recent weeks, launching repeated strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport. One such strike killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, making it the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.
Saudi Arabia has looked for military support from regional and Western allies to counter the intensified Houthi attacks. France agreed to deploy defense assets, including military personnel, and more than 100 American military advisers are on the ground providing intelligence and targeting support under a newly established joint forces command.
Pakistan has forces stationed in Saudi Arabia, and the Egyptian parliament is debating whether to send support after President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi called an emergency session to deploy military assistance to the kingdom.
“The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable,” UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said in a statement. “The targeting of the airport in Riyadh in particular shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region.”
Last month, the Iran-allied rebel group launched a lightning offensive on Yemen’s western coast, capturing key territory. That included the Bab al-Mandeb maritime chokepoint on the Red Sea, potentially expanding Tehran’s influence over another trade corridor.
Saudi Arabia cancels next week’s ‘Davos in the Desert’ conference after series of Houthi attacks
Backed by Saudi warplanes, Yemen’s anti-Houthi government ground forces have launched a counteroffensive to recapture lost territory. Despite a heavy airstrike campaign and a large ground offensive, Houthi rebels have retained control over key locations and have continued launching missiles and drones at their adversaries.
At least 53 newly recruited Yemeni government forces were killed by the Houthis in a ballistic missile attack Monday on the southeastern Shabwa province, local officials said. More than 200 others were reported wounded.
The attack was condemned by the US mission to Yemen, which called it a “cowardly attack by the Iran-backed Houthi militia” on Yemenis who had “volunteered to keep their communities and country safe.”
This story has been updated with additional developments.
James Frater contributed reporting

articles.title_orig: Hegseth Said to Make Unannounced Visit to Israel for Talks With Netanyahu
articles.title_zh: Hegseth Said to Make Unannounced Visit to Israel for Talks With Netanyahu
articles.content_orig:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth discussed Iran with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an unannounced visit to Israel on Monday, three Israeli officials said, as tensions flare between the U.S. and Iran .
Doron Spielman, a spokesperson for the prime minister, later confirmed to Reuters that Netanyahu had met with Hegseth at the Uvda Air Force Base in Israel’s southern Negev desert region.
Netanyahu and Hegseth discussed “the threats in the region” and the U.S.-Israel partnership in dealing both offensively and defensively with those threats, he said in a brief phone call.
Hegseth also thanked Israel for hosting U.S. forces, which Spielman said numbered in the thousands, and discussed President Donald Trump’s support for the prime minister.
“There’s a deep personal relationship here that was at the core of this discussion,” Spielman said.
On Sunday, Trump endorsed Netanyahu in next week’s parliamentary election in Israel, the country’s first ballot since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack on southern Israel.
The Pentagon has not publicly commented on Hegseth’s visit.
Hegseth earlier posted on X that he had visited U.S. service members in the Central Command area of responsibility, which covers the Middle East, northeast Africa and parts of Asia.
He did not specify where he had met with the forces.
Hegseth’s visit comes as tensions flare between the U.S. and Iran over the Strait of Hormuz and as Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthis intensify their attacks on Saudi Arabia.
U.S. and Israeli forces launched joint strikes against Iran in late February, setting off the wider Middle East war. Netanyahu told Israeli media this month that he’s not seeking to attack Iran before the Oct. 27 Israeli election. Trump has said he will not attack Iran before U.S. midterm elections in November.
Israel has hosted additional U.S. forces, including military aircraft, since at least February as part of the war with Iran.

articles.title_orig: Trump Tariffs on Canada Spark Latest Lawsuit Over Trade Powers
articles.title_zh: Trump Tariffs on Canada Spark Latest Lawsuit Over Trade Powers
articles.content_orig:
A new lawsuit filed Tuesday challenges President Donald Trump 's invocation of a Depression-era law to impose 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods .
Trump in July used Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to slap those steep tariffs on Canadian hockey sticks, wine, honey, wigs, and other products in response to alleged trade discrimination by Ottawa. It was the first time the 96-year-old law had ever been used to impose a tariff.
"Section 338 is a relic of the retaliation-based tariff policy" that has been "impliedly repealed" by subsequent legislation, the civil complaint filed in the U.S. Court of International Trade says.
The suit was filed by Gellert Global Group, a New Jersey-based food importer that says its cheeses are covered by the tariffs. The complaint asks the court to declare the tariffs unlawful, block their enforcement, and order the Trump administration to issue refunds for duties already paid, with interest.
Gellert Global is represented by the Liberty Justice Center, the same legal group that dealt a major blow to Trump's trade agenda by successfully contesting his "reciprocal" tariffs.
The Supreme Court struck those tariffs down in February. The administration is in the process of refunding the estimated $166 billion that the federal government collected from importers through the reciprocal duties.
The Liberty Justice Center is currently engaged in two other lawsuits against what it says is Trump's misuse of laws to impose sweeping tariffs.
"This case is not about the president. It is about the presidency," the group's CEO Sara Albrecht said in a statement Tuesday morning announcing Gellert Global's suit. "No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required."
The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on the suit.

articles.title_orig: Zelenskyy meets with Trump envoys as U.S. blasts ‘scandalous’ accusations on withdrawn support
articles.title_zh: Zelenskyy meets with Trump envoys as U.S. blasts ‘scandalous’ accusations on withdrawn support
articles.content_orig:
U.S. envoys were meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday, as Kyiv scrambled to respond to an American pressure campaign that has been allied with moves aimed at courting the Kremlin.
President Donald Trump’s negotiators, son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, have so far had little success finding a diplomatic solution to the war . Their latest meeting comes with Washington’s backing in doubt as Kyiv accused the U.S. of withdrawing support crucial to its defense against Russia — a suggestion that Secretary of State Marco Rubio called “scandalous.”
Witkoff had been set to meet with Zelenskyy in Oslo, with Kushner joining via videoconference, the Norwegian government said earlier. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb was also joining the talks, it added.
Officials from the U.S. and Ukraine had been expected to meet in Norway this week for another round of negotiations, sources familiar with the matter told NBC News, as a series of recent actions by Trump in favor of Russia left both Congress and U.S. allies questioning U.S. mediation efforts.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters he hoped that it would be possible for Trump’s envoys to hold a meeting in Russia “in the near future,” though he gave no firm indication on when this might be.
Trump has waived sanctions and agreed a diesel deal with Russia, in an apparent bid to lower fuel prices ahead of the Midterm elections. He called Monday for Zelenskyy to “get somebody else to negotiate,” his latest rebuke of the Ukrainian president.
Trump also appeared to downplay the impact of Russian attacks on Ukraine, a near-daily reality for the last 4 ½ years that have killed scores of civilians and flattened towns.
“Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine,” Trump told reporters. “They haven’t been doing much.”
It was the latest public sign of his shift away from Ukraine.
Kyiv said it had once again received no early warning from the U.S. before the capital came under attack by Russian ballistic missiles on Sunday, the third time in recent days.
In addition to the withholding of intelligence, Ukraine said it was still facing speed restrictions on Starshield, the military version of the SpaceX service, with no explanation from the American side.
“All of this suggests that some political decision has been made to slow down support for us,” Zelenskyy said Monday in a virtual address to a bipartisan Congressional delegation. He also said the U.S. was delaying the delivery of crucial ballistic missile interceptors, and that Ukraine has nearly run out of its supplies.
Zelenskyy said early Tuesday he held “a substantive conversation” with Rubio, focusing on missile interceptors, early warnings of ballistic attacks and Starshield restrictions. He thanked Rubio and “everyone in America who supports fair approaches.”
Rubio told reporters later that he told Zelenskyy in the 45-minute call that nothing had changed in U.S. support for Ukraine.
“There’s nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine,” he added, speaking at the start of a trip to India.
When it comes to missile interceptors, Rubio said the U.S. has to strike a delicate balance between its obligations to other partners and its own requirements when it comes to what he called “the most in-demand product” in the defense industry right now.
“When a country doesn’t get interceptors from the United States, it’s not because we are denying,” he added. “We have our own needs too.”
Ukrainian officials including Zelenskyy have made clear their accusation that the U.S. has imposed restrictions that have disrupted military operations and hampered Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian missiles, making the attacks more deadly.
“That’s scandalous, that’s outrageous, that’s just simply not true. That’s not accurate,” Rubio said Tuesday.
Officials in the eastern Kharkiv region shared images Monday of a dead child in a stroller — a one-year-old girl they said was killed alongside her mother in a Russian attack on a public park in the region.
“ The world has enough strength to stop the war. That strength must finally be used — against the murderers,” Zelenskyy said in a post decrying the strike.
Yuliya Talmazan is a reporter for NBC News Digital, based in London.
Abigail Williams is a producer and reporter for NBC News covering the State Department.

articles.content_orig:

A Massachusetts-based manufacturer has recalled more than 1.5 million pounds of various meat products over serious potential health concerns.
Kayem Foods Inc. initiated the recall after learning that the items may not have been stored at the correct temperature. It has since been deemed a Class I recall by the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Food Safety and Inspection Service, meaning “there is a reasonable probability that the use of the product will cause serious, adverse health consequences or death.”
An investigation that began after a customer reported receiving a warm product delivery on October 1 revealed that a warehouse cooler experienced temperature fluctuations while storing the items, according to FSIS.
Approximately 1,584,361 recalled items were manufactured between March 31, 2026 and October 7, 2026 and are labeled with the establishment numbers “EST. M/P 7839,” “EST. P 20935A” or “EST. M 9520” inside the USDA inspection mark. Affected items were shipped to retail and food service locations across the U.S. and Hong Kong.
Products include various brands of hot dogs, bacon, sausage, and deli meat. A full list of affected items can be found here .
There have been no reports of illness, but customers in possession of recalled products should discard them or return them to the place of purchase.
The meat recall comes amid a slew of issues affecting consumers.
Over 112,000 bottles of pain relievers sold by Amazon were voluntarily recalled last week due to discoloration. The news was shared in an enforcement report from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration .
Various bottles of 500-milligram Extra Strength Acetaminophen caplets sold across the U.S. have been affected. Customer complaints about discolored tablets led to the voluntary recall initiated by Amazon, according to the report.
Included in the recall are 90,456 500-count bottles, 14,640 200-count bottles, and 7,836 1000-count bottles, all with various lot numbers and expiration dates between September 30, 2027 and February 29, 2028.
No injuries or adverse health effects related to the discoloration of the tablets have been reported.
Amazon has contacted customers who have purchased affected bottles for refund information. Customers can check their order history and product lot numbers on Amazon’s website .
A pre-workout powder has also been recalled after it was found to contain an illegal and dangerous stimulant , the FDA said last week.
A batch of “Leader Formulas, LLC RAPTURE Preworkout” sold online and in stores between January 2025 and May 2026 was made with “1,3-Dimethylamylamine,” also known as “ DMAA .”
DMAA is a synthetic chemical developed from amphetamine, sometimes used in dietary supplements that can spike blood pressure and lead to heart attacks, shortness of breath and tightening of the chest.

articles.title_orig: The manosphere stars who helped Trump win are losing their shine
articles.title_zh: The manosphere stars who helped Trump win are losing their shine
articles.content_orig:

“I’m embarrassed on a world stage,” said a regretful Trump voter in a Navigator Research focus group shared first with The 19th.
Two years ago, six White suburban mothers were among the more than 77 million Americans who voted to put President Donald Trump back in the White House. Now, they say they regret it.
In a recent focus group convened by Navigator Research, a Democratic polling and public opinion firm, and shared exclusively with The 19th, the six Trump voters discussed their disappointment with his second term — and their mixed feelings about the upcoming midterm elections. Navigator shared the group with The 19th on the condition that the participants be referred to only by their first names to protect their privacy.
Chrissy, a 44-year-old woman from Michigan, said that two years ago, she was “lazy” in basing her vote on political ads and discussions with others instead of her own research.
The 19th thanks our sponsors. Become one .
Now, she’s committed to voting for candidates who will check Trump.
“He’s pushed the country into an authoritarian playbook,” she said. “And if we don’t do something to stop it right now, it’s unlikely that there’ll be much left.”
Trump is also losing women who were once among his most committed backers.
“I was a die-hard supporter, but it’s been a complete backstab since, pretty much, the storming of the Capitol for me,” said Kristen, a 39-year-old woman in Ohio. “That’s when my opinion really started changing about how he is as a leader.”
Nicole, a 47-year-old in Texas, could relate. She believes Trump “might have his intentions in the right place,” but his second term hasn’t matched his campaign promises. She knows people struggling to afford groceries and turning to public assistance programs to make ends meet, and she thinks things “will get worse before they get better.”
“I just feel we’re drowning, and it only started when Trump got in office,” she said. “I was fully, like she said, a die-hard fan of Trump. I mean, flag supporter, everything. Now I feel like I regret voting for him, I’ll just be honest.”
Melissa Toufanian, a managing director at Navigator, said their research has found that 1 in 4 people who voted for Trump in 2024 now regret it. Moms are more likely to regret their votes than dads — and suburban women are a critical election demographic for both parties.
While all the focus group participants have soured on Trump, they aren’t all sold on Democrats. Several expressed deep disillusionment with politics and doubted their votes could meaningfully change what they see as a broken status quo upheld by both political parties.
“I do think in a lot of ways that our voice doesn’t matter anymore,” said Gayle, a 47-year-old in Florida. “I think Congress sucks, honestly. I just think it sucks. I don’t think that they’re in it for the people. I think they’re in it for themselves these days, and it’s really on both sides.”
The cost of living consistently ranks as voters’ top concern, and many Democratic candidates are putting affordability front and center in their campaigns. Polling from The 19th and YouGov found that women are more worried than men about paying for groceries, healthcare, housing and retirement.
Even women who weren’t as personally affected by rising prices saw the war in Iran and the resulting increase in gas and fuel prices as a clear about-face from Trump’s 2024 campaign promises to lower costs.
“I’m not struggling, but so many people are,” said Denise, a 49-year-old woman from Ohio. “I’m repulsed about the tariffs that we’ve put on our neighbor in Canada, the war, basically picking on other countries and just starting a war for no reason.”
Of the entire group, Gayle had the most positive assessment of Trump’s second term and the economy. But she said she regretted voting for him because of the war in Iran, which “really messed things up.”
“If you’re looking at the gas prices versus if I’m going to see a nuclear bomb happen, I’m more concerned with my gas prices than I am with the nuclear bomb, to be honest,” she said.
And it wasn’t just the economy that made the women in the focus group turn against Trump.
Denise pointed to Trump “taking down history because he’s a narcissist” in tearing down the East Wing of the White House to build a new ballroom.
“It just … that disgusts me,” she said. “He had no right to do that, and that’s one of the big things that pissed me off.”
Women in the focus group said that while they supported enforcing immigration laws and securing the border, they thought the government had gone too far.
“I’m not against the deportation, I’m against inhumane treatment in that process,” said Kristen, the 39-year-old in Ohio.
Brandy, a 43-year-old woman in North Carolina, said she was particularly troubled by federal immigration officials killing two U.S. citizens , Renee Good and Alex Pretti, in Minnesota. She said when she posted about Good’s killing on Facebook, she was attacked by her friends who are “extreme Trump lovers.”
“He just makes people lose their human decency,” she said.
And they didn’t view other members of the Trump administration much more favorably. They used words like “terrible,” “compromised,” “Trump’s twin,” and “corrupt” to describe Vice President JD Vance. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was called “a liar,” and Robert F. Kennedy Jr.  “uneducated.” Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth “should have stayed on TV,” Kristen said.
But despite the group’s collective distaste for Trump and his inner circle, not all plan to vote for Democrats down the ballot in November.
Denise in Ohio said she was leaning toward voting for Democrat Amy Acton in Ohio’s race for governor over Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, whom she described as “up [Trump’s] rear end,” while Gayle in Florida said she planned to vote for the Republican, Rep. Byron Donalds, in her state’s gubernatorial race.
Brandy said she didn’t like former Gov. Roy Cooper, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in North Carolina, but was voting for him because of GOP nominee Michael Whatley’s ties to a convicted sex offender who served in several leadership positions in the state Republican Party, something Democratic groups have spent millions highlighting in campaign ads.
“I’m gonna go for the guy that doesn’t have a buddy that’s a sex offender,” she said. “Even though I don’t like him, he is the lesser of two evils.”
Toufanian said Democrats have a big opportunity to focus on issues suburban women care about “and to really make some tangible improvements in their lives.”
Food quality and safety is one of those issues. Nearly all the women cited it as a top concern, but only two had heard of the acronym MAHA, or Make America Healthy Again .
“I think there’s a real opportunity because it touches on so many of the other issues that are so important in this election cycle, particularly corruption and affordability,” Toufanian said.
Most women in the focus group said they’re taking a wait-and-see approach to the 2028 presidential race. Two, Chrissy and Kristen, said they were open to voting for a Democrat but wouldn’t want to vote for Vance or former Vice President Kamala Harris, the 2024 Democratic presidential nominee.
Chrissy said she’d primarily evaluate Republican candidates on whether they would further the “cruelty” and “highly polarized” atmosphere cultivated by Trump.

articles.title_orig: Apple explains why HomeView couldn’t launch until now
articles.title_zh: Apple explains why HomeView couldn’t launch until now
articles.content_orig:
Apple’s new HomeView was reportedly mostly finished for years, but kept getting delayed. Here’s why HomeView couldn’t launch until now, per quotes from key Apple execs.
In November 2024, Mark Gurman published an in-depth report on the product we now know as HomeView. At the time, he said Apple was targeting a March 2025 launch. But that date kept slipping, and now HomeView will finally arrive in homes on November 13, 2026.
Why the long wait? Gurman has repeatedly pointed to Siri AI as the chief cause of delays. And Apple execs have now largely confirmed that in quotes given to The Verge .
Jennifer Pattison Tuohy asked Kaiann Drance, Apple’s VP of product marketing for home, why now was the right time for HomeView and Apple’s renewed smart home push.
She said Siri AI and the personal context it brings, which she called Apple’s “privacy story,” came together with a device designed specifically for the home. “With the magic of Siri AI, it comes together in a way that we haven’t been able to deliver before,” she said.
HomeView is being marketed as a shared device that taps into users’ personal context in a way that wasn’t possible pre-Siri AI. So it’s easy to see how Apple’s main pitch would need to change without the more personalized Siri.
A similar explanation was given by Apple’s Lilian Rincon, VP of product marketing for AI. She told The Verge that Siri AI is core to HomeView because it’s “much more capable” and also highlighted its conversational abilities, which make it easy to use for any family member.
“It’s great because you can just ask it to change the temperature on your thermostat in a very natural way. As the Siri AI capabilities continue to evolve, the home experience is fitting to be able to interact with in this natural way.” On why now, Rincon says the natural-language shift is the point where AI goes mainstream. “Because now it can be … my mother-in-law or the Gen Z who’s in college, both of them can use this in the way that they naturally speak and get what they want.”
This emphasis and explanation also makes HomeView’s absence in the EU more understandable.
If Siri AI was simply a nice-to-have addition to an otherwise feature-rich product, perhaps it could launch in the EU still. But if the whole value proposition revolves around the new assistant and its personalized features, waiting until Siri AI is available for iOS in the EU makes more sense.
You can read The Verge’s full article here for more quotes and context.
What do you think of Apple’s explanation for the HomeView’s launch timing? Let us know in the comments.

Insatiable demand for artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure has been a generational catalyst for memory specialist Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU). After an extraordinary rally earlier this year, investors may be wondering where the stock is headed next.
Between 2020 and 2025, Micron stock generated an average gain of 28% during the calendar fourth quarter. So far this year, the story has looked different. After closing September at $1,065, Micron stock has fallen roughly 17% through Oct. 16.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
Nevertheless, I see two upcoming catalysts that could help reverse sentiment and send Micron shares soaring before 2027 arrives.
Over the next several weeks, investors will hear from some of the world's largest AI companies. Space Exploration Technologies reports third-quarter earnings on Oct. 20, followed by Tesla and Meta Platforms on Oct. 21. Microsoft , Alphabet , Amazon , Apple , and Nvidia are also scheduled to report earnings throughout the remainder of October and November.
These earnings reports could be especially important for Micron because each of these companies is spending hundreds of billions of dollars building AI data centers, and they are increasingly discussing the same bottleneck: memory supply.
During SpaceX's second-quarter earnings call, Elon Musk said memory was the limiting factor for AI development. He implied that memory production was growing 20% annually while demand was increasing much faster, around 200%. His outlook was straightforward: "Economics 101 would suggest that the price increases."
Musk has also publicly praised Micron for being reasonable about memory prices, suggesting that the company's approach will strengthen customer relationships.
Meanwhile, Apple's former CEO Tim Cook touched on memory costs during the company's July earnings call. Cook characterized the situation as a "hundred-year flood," explaining why Apple decided to raise prices on certain products.
These comments are important because they illustrate how memory shortages aren't limited to data centers. Demand for high bandwidth memory (HBM) and advanced DRAM also affects consumer electronics, autonomous systems, and other end-markets.
As big tech companies continue discussing their capital expenditure (capex) plans, investors will likely receive additional evidence that memory supply remains tight. For Micron, that could reinforce expectations for higher average selling prices and stronger profitability heading into next year.
On Oct. 8, Micron's board increased the company's share repurchase authorization to $35.16 billion. The timing of this announcement was particularly interesting. During Micron's most recent earnings call, CFO Mark Murphy explained that the company will increase capital returns beginning Dec. 9, subject to restrictions associated with CHIPS Act funding agreements.
When a company repurchases stock, it reduces the number of outstanding shares. That means future earnings are divided among fewer shares, potentially increasing earnings per share (EPS) even without additional profit growth.
Considering Micron is already witnessing record earnings momentum, stock buybacks should provide another tailwind. If the company begins repurchasing shares while its valuation remains depressed, the new authorization could prove especially lucrative for long-term investors.
The most compelling part of Micron's investment thesis revolves around valuation. Wall Street's fiscal 2027 earnings estimates currently sit around $176 per share. With Micron trading around $911, that implies a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of roughly 5.2. That's a reasonable multiple for a company benefiting from one of the AI industry's biggest investment cycles.
Of course, there are reasons for investors to be cautious. Memory is notoriously cyclical. If manufacturers expand production too aggressively, prices could eventually decline. Moreover, rising competition from China's ChangXin Memory Technologies ( CXMT ) also presents a longer-term risk.
Nevertheless, Micron's near-term fundamentals are compelling. The company has secured numerous long-term strategic customer agreements that cover a substantial portion of its expected fiscal 2027 production, which provides greater visibility into future demand.
When combined with favorable industry conditions and Micron's expanded buyback authorization, the bull case becomes clear. Investors could see rising earnings, a shrinking share count, and potentially an expanding valuation multiple if confidence in the memory industry's outlook improves.
In turn, Micron stock could witness substantial stock-price appreciation sooner than most investors anticipate. In my view, Micron's recent sell-off presents an attractive entry point ahead of 2027. With shares trading at a reasonable valuation, I see Micron stock as a rock-solid buy for long-term investors.

articles.title_orig: Global oil prices hit highest level in 5 months amid attacks on ships, facilities - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Global oil prices hit highest level in 5 months amid attacks on ships, facilities - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Global oil prices have climbed more than 55% since the outbreak of the Iran war.
Global oil prices climbed to their highest level in five months on Tuesday after Iran and its Houthi allies claimed attacks on oil infrastructure in the Middle East.
The Brent crude futures price, a benchmark for global trading, topped $111 a barrel for the first time since May before retreating to $110.30 a barrel. The latest reading marks a rise of more than 55% since the Iran war began in late February.
An oil shortage continues to bedevil crude sellers, who typically pass along elevated costs to refiners, leading to higher prices at the pump.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center, or UKMTO, on Tuesday issued an advisory after it received a report of an incident involving a tanker and military forces off the coast of Oman.
Separately, Iranian state-run media reported on Tuesday that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed that two oil tankers hit naval mines south of the Strait of Hormuz.
The reports came a day after Yemen-based Houthi militants claimed a wave of strikes on Saudia Arabia on Monday, including the Shaybah oil field as well as Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu, a port city near a key transport corridor on the Red Sea.
The West Texas Intermediate futures price, a benchmark index for U.S. trading, also jumped on Tuesday. The price of U.S. oil prices stands at $105.75, a rise of more than 60% since the outbreak of the war.
The jump in oil prices arrived as affordability marks a top concern for voters ahead of early November's midterm elections .
The average price of a gallon of gas in the U.S. clocked in at $4.27 on Tuesday, according to AAA . That figure amounts to a rise of nearly $1.30 since the start late February.
The Middle East conflict drove up fuel prices and catapulted U.S. inflation to a three-year high in May, but inflation eased slightly over the summer after a preliminary peace agreement established an on-again, off-again pause in fighting.
The tentative accord between the U.S. and Iran expired in August, giving way to continued attacks on oil infrastructure and ships in the region.
The U.S. -- the world's largest oil producer -- imports a small amount of crude from the Middle East. Since oil and gas are sold on a global market, however, the shortage has sent prices rising for everyone, including U.S. drivers.
ABC News' Nasser Atta, Othon Leyva and Desiree Adib contributed to this report.

US stocks climbed on Tuesday as chip stocks trimmed losses and investors turned their focus to a slew of earnings out this week.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) rose 0.9%, and the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) gained 0.4%. The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) erased its decline, climbing 0.2% after the major averages closed mixed on Monday, as tech stocks rebounded.
The AI trade came into focus on Tuesday after Elice ( 0158S0.KQ ), a South Korean data center provider, saw its shares plunge 32% during its public debut in Seoul, underscoring lingering concerns about the health of the AI trade.
Investors turned their attention to a fresh round of corporate earnings this week. General Motors ( GM ) tightened its profit outlook but announced a $20 billion share buyback program . United Airlines ( UAL ) will report after the close.
Streaming giant Netflix ( NFLX ) will report quarterly earnings after the bell on Tuesday. EV maker Tesla ( TSLA ) and social media giant Meta ( META ) are expected to post results on Wednesday.
On the economic front, housing starts fell to a four-month low amid soft demand, with mortgage rates remaining elevated.
Brent crude futures ( BZ=F ) fell to $108 per barrel while West Texas Intermediate crude ( CL=F ) traded below $98.
Qualcomm ( QCOM ) shares rose 1% following a report that the designer of chips for smartphones plans to start cutting jobs globally next month as part of a "performance-focused reduction" following employee reviews.
The plan was outlined in a memo to staff from CEO Cristiano Amon, which Reuters reviewed. Notifications are set to start in November.
The memo did not specify how many positions would be affected.
Qualcomm shares are up more than 2% year-to-date.
Wall Street is in a buying mood. The AI trade's leaders had to bleed a little before joining in.
The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) slipped below Friday's close early, giving back Monday's rebound from an eight-session losing streak, as my colleague Ines Ferré reported . Then buyers showed up right at the summer floor near 11,000.
Chart watchers know this setup.
A dip below support that quickly reverses is a bear trap , catching traders who bet on a breakdown. But it only counts if chips close back above Friday's level.
And history says don't relax yet. After every losing streak of seven sessions or more since 1994, the index traded below the streak's final close within a month. After the longest ones, it was lower a month later most of the time.
A BofA Global Research report calls last week's rout a "positioning-driven hiccup on the fringes of the AI trade." The credit market isn't so sure. The cost of insuring Oracle's debt is at its highest since at least 2021, and even the megacaps' default swaps are creeping up.
A close above 11,137 springs the trap. Lose 11,000, and the next stop is closer to 10,450.
US stocks were mixed at Tuesday's open as investors weighed another batch of corporate earnings against pressure from higher government bond yields.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) rose 0.4% while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) fell 0.1%. The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) declined 0.5% after the major averages closed mixed on Monday as tech stocks rebounded.
Investors remain focused on whether strong third-quarter earnings can keep stocks moving higher after last week's volatility. At Tuesday's open the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield ( ^TNX ) hovered at 5.10%, keeping pressure on stock valuations though easing over the last week.
AI infrastructure stocks are under pressure again before the opening bell. CoreWeave ( CRWV ) is taking the hardest hit.
The AI cloud provider is trading at its lowest level since May 2025 premarket, extending a slide of more than 40% since Oct. 6.
So what's spooking investors? The debt. CoreWeave borrowed heavily to build its data centers, and its bonds sold off across maturities last week, as my colleague Brian Sozzi reported .
Siebert Financial chief investment officer Mark Malek isn't rushing in. Some AI stocks are "honestly down for the right reason," he said Monday on Yahoo Finance's Market Hang. He "wouldn't back up the truck."
Every chip stock trading premarket in a 60-stock Yahoo Finance semiconductor basket is lower, with SK hynix ( SKHY ) and Nebius ( NBIS ) among the hardest hit. The rest of the market is calmer, with S&P 500 gainers outnumbering decliners roughly 3 to 2.
Monday's low of $59.25 is the line in the sand. A snap back above it would make this breakdown a bear trap — a fake-out that burns traders betting on more losses.
Stay below, and the next stops are around $53, then the all-time low at $33 and change.
Yahoo Finance's Pras Subramanian reports:
GM ( GM ) posted third quarter results before the bell that topped estimates. The automaker tightened its full-year profit outlook instead of boosting it, but issued shareholders a new $20 billion share repurchase program instead.
For the quarter, GM posted Q3 revenue of $50.0 billion, up 2.9% from a year ago and above the $48.52 billion Bloomberg consensus. GM posted adjusted EPS of $3.70 vs $3.57 estimated, with adjusted EBIT coming in at $4.1 billion, ahead of the $4.02 billion expected and up nearly 22%.
President Trump announced an $8 billion aid package on Monday to help US farmers pay for diesel this harvest season.
The relief program, announced at a campaign rally in Kansas and on social media, aims to bring down fuel costs for Americans ahead of next month's midterm elections.
"Tonight, I am also pleased to announce that the Department of Agriculture will be launching a new 'Harvest Fuel Relief Program,' providing our Farmers with 8 BILLION DOLLARS in support to offset Diesel costs during this Harvest Season," Trump's account posted on Truth Social ( DJT ).

articles.title_orig: US single-family housing starts plunge; building permits hit 3-1/2-year low
articles.title_zh: US single-family housing starts plunge; building permits hit 3-1/2-year low
articles.content_orig:
New residential construction declined in September to one of the weakest paces since the pandemic and building permits for single-family homes slid, highlighting a languishing housing market.
Housing starts decreased 5.2% to an annualized rate of 1.22 million, a four-month low, according to federal government data released Tuesday. The pace trailed all estimates in a Bloomberg survey of economists.
Starts of single-family homes decreased to the lowest level in a year, and applications for permits on those dwellings — a gauge of future construction — dropped to the lowest since early 2023.
The residential real estate market is being constrained by affordability challenges now further compounded by higher mortgage rates.
Homebuilders, whose confidence has slumped to a 14-year low, may also be reluctant to begin construction on new homes before making more progress on inventories.
The report showed new construction on multifamily projects, which include apartments and can be volatile on a monthly basis, fell nearly 7%.
Sluggish home construction has weighed on economic growth in five of the last six quarters.
Before Tuesday’s report, the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta’s GDPNow forecast penciled in residential investment declining an annualized 1.3% in the third quarter.
Completions of single-family homes last month dropped to the weakest pace in more than six years.
Starts of one-family homes in the South, the nation’s largest homebuilding region, dropped to the lowest level since January. They also fell in the West and Midwest.
The new residential construction data are volatile, and the government report showed 90% confidence that the total monthly change ranged from a 17% decline to a 6.6% gain.

A beat-and-raise quarter from GE Aerospace ( NYSE:GE ) is running into a jump in engine-related costs. GE Aerospace stock fell 4%, landing at $299.59 during the morning session, even after the jet engine maker topped estimates and raised its full-year outlook.
Meanwhile, RTX ( NYSE:RTX ) stock is up 0.52% to $193.15. The gap stands out because both companies sell engines into the same commercial aviation market, pointing to a selloff rooted in GE Aerospace's own quarter.
On the surface, GE Aerospace delivered a clean quarter. Its Q3 2026 adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of $2.25 beat the $1.99 consensus estimate, and revenue of $14.12 billion topped the $12.84 billion analysts expected.
Management raised GE Aerospace's full-year 2026 guidance across the board. That outlook now calls for adjusted EPS of $8 to $8.10, up from a prior range of $7.65 to $7.85. Targets for operating profit and free cash flow moved higher as well.
Beneath those headline figures, GE Aerospace's costs are climbing fast. GE Aerospace's sales discounts and allowances rose sharply on new engine installations, spare parts and durability reserves. The company's cash generation slid too, with free cash flow falling 9.2% year over year to $2.04 billion while operating income barely moved at $2.81 billion.
Many successful investors eventually reach the same moment. The saving is done, the portfolio is built, and the question quietly changes from how much can I grow this to how much can I take out? Get that second question wrong and decades of good investing can come apart in a handful of years.

Mix and inflation also weighed on GE Aerospace margins, partially offsetting gains from higher volume and pricing. Separately, the company deferred revenue recognition on its GE9X engine pending midseal certification, which adds one more open question to an already complex cost story.
Chief executive H. Lawrence Culp Jr. struck an upbeat tone as GE Aerospace posted its results. "Thanks to the collaboration of the GE Aerospace team with our supplier partners we continue to build momentum," Culp stated. He also pointed to record internal shop visit output and an agreement to acquire Consolidated Precision Products, a castings supplier, to expand capacity.
GE Aerospace now expects commercial services revenue to grow at a low-double-digit rate in 2027. That forecast rests on what Culp called the company's "over $170 billion commercial services backlog," which gives the services business deep visibility into future work.
Demand is holding firm at GE Aerospace, with total orders up 49% to $19 billion in the quarter. Its commercial services orders climbed 23%, and the company keeps spending over $3 billion a year on research and development.
GE Aerospace makes most of its profit servicing commercial jet engines over their working lives, while RTX pairs its engines with defense systems. Boeing ( NYSE:BA ) builds the aircraft those engines power. A service-heavy model like GE Aerospace's puts parts allowances and durability reserves close to the center of its earnings, which helps explain why the cost jump hurts. Boeing shares are down 0.49% to $190.57.
Across the sector, the iShares U.S. Aerospace & Defense ETF ( CBOE:ITA ) is down 0.4% to $206.90. That far smaller decline marks the GE Aerospace stock selloff as company-specific.
Furthermore, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:SPY ) is down by only 0.1% to $765.92. With the broad market nearly flat, macro weakness explains little of the slide in GE Aerospace shares.

As long as those costs keep climbing, GE Aerospace stock could stay volatile around each quarterly report. Position sizes should stay small until GE Aerospace's cost picture resolves.
